title: Chapter 5 Drill: Esophagus, Stomach, Small Intestine, and Endoscopy

items.stem: A 71-year-old man in the intensive care unit after cardiac surgery is on two vasopressors and a high-dose inotrope. He develops abdominal distension, rising lactate, and bloody stool. Angiography shows a patent main mesenteric artery with diffuse narrowing and alternating dilation of branch vessels. What is the best initial management?
options: Reduce vasopressors where possible and infuse intra-arterial papaverine
Emergency mesenteric embolectomy through the superior mesenteric artery
Long-term anticoagulation and surgical bypass to the superior mesenteric artery
Intravenous thrombolysis for venous clot
items.explanation: Nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia results from splanchnic vasoconstriction in low-flow states, and the main vessels are patent with a characteristic beaded appearance of branches. Treatment is to correct the underlying low flow, minimize vasoconstrictors, and give intra-arterial vasodilator such as papaverine, with laparotomy if peritonitis develops. Embolectomy, bypass, and thrombolysis treat occlusive disease, not vasospasm. Papaverine is continued for a period, with repeat angiography to confirm the response.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has brisk hematochezia, a heart rate of 128, a blood pressure of 82/50 mm Hg, and a blood urea nitrogen level that is disproportionately raised compared with creatinine. He responds partially to resuscitation. What is the next step?
options: Urgent colonoscopy without bowel preparation as the first study
Upper endoscopy after resuscitation, as the source may be upper
Technetium-labeled red cell scan before any endoscopic evaluation
Barium swallow and small bowel follow-through before any endoscopy
items.explanation: Hemodynamic instability with hematochezia and an elevated urea-to-creatinine ratio suggests a brisk upper source, since blood is a protein load and rapid transit produces red stool. Upper endoscopy after resuscitation is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Unprepared colonoscopy yields poor views, and a nuclear scan delays treatment of an unstable patient. Barium studies are not used for acute bleeding.

items.stem: On the second day after Ivor Lewis esophagectomy, a 61-year-old man has worsening hypotension and a lactate of 6.2 mmol per liter. Bedside endoscopy shows black, necrotic mucosa in the gastric conduit extending beyond the anastomosis. What is the best next step?
options: Continue observation with nasogastric decompression, antibiotics, and a repeat endoscopy
Endoscopic stent placement across the anastomosis with enteral feeding
Percutaneous drainage of the mediastinum with continued antibiotics only
Urgent reoperation with resection of the necrotic conduit and cervical diversion
items.explanation: Early conduit necrosis is a surgical emergency. Diffuse necrosis beyond the anastomosis will not recover and leads to sepsis and perforation, so the dead conduit must be resected, the proximal esophagus diverted in the neck, and enteral access placed, with reconstruction months later. Stents and drains are used for viable but leaking anastomoses. Observation under antibiotics is unsafe.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has painless bright red blood per rectum. Her pulse is 88 and blood pressure is 134/80 mm Hg, and hemoglobin is 11.2 g/dL. There is no use of anticoagulants. Which is the best initial diagnostic approach?
options: Colonoscopy after rapid bowel preparation within 24 hours
Immediate surgical exploration with on-table enteroscopy
Barium enema before any form of endoscopy is attempted
Outpatient colonoscopy in six weeks after bleeding stops
items.explanation: In a stable patient with acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding, colonoscopy after a rapid purge, ideally within 24 hours, identifies the source and allows treatment. Emergency laparotomy is reserved for instability with failed localization. Barium blocks later endoscopy and cannot treat the lesion. A six-week delay is unsafe for ongoing bleeding and misses the chance of therapy.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has episodic crushing chest pain and intermittent dysphagia to both solids and liquids. Barium swallow shows a corkscrew esophagus. Manometry shows normal lower esophageal sphincter relaxation and premature, rapidly propagated contractions in many swallows. What is the diagnosis?
options: Type I achalasia with absent contractility and failed sphincter relaxation
Distal esophageal spasm with premature contractions and a relaxing sphincter
Scleroderma esophagus with a hypotensive sphincter and weak peristalsis
Jackhammer esophagus with elevated contractile vigor and normal latency
items.explanation: Normal sphincter relaxation with premature contractions defines distal esophageal spasm. Achalasia requires failed relaxation. Scleroderma produces weak or absent peristalsis and a patulous, hypotensive sphincter. Jackhammer esophagus is defined by excessive contractile amplitude rather than short latency. Treatment starts with acid suppression and smooth muscle relaxants, with myotomy reserved for refractory, severe cases. High-resolution manometry is the test that separates these patterns.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman with dysphagia after a stroke has her percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube fall out on day 4. The skin site looks clean and she has no pain. What should be done?
options: Reinsert a new tube through the site at the bedside and begin feeding
Cover the site and wait until the tract matures to replace it in ten days
Avoid blind reinsertion; confirm the tract and replace under guidance
Insert a nasogastric tube and take no further action regarding the tract
items.explanation: An immature tract in the first one to two weeks has not yet fused the stomach to the abdominal wall, so blind replacement can place the tube in the peritoneum and cause peritonitis. The tract and tube position must be confirmed by contrast study or endoscopy, or a new gastrostomy placed. Simply waiting may leave her without nutrition and the tract closing, and ignoring a possible leak is unsafe.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has severe constant abdominal pain, a heart rate of 118, and a white count of 17,000 per microliter. Computed tomography shows a U-shaped dilated loop with a mesenteric swirl, mesenteric fluid, and reduced wall enhancement. What is the best management?
options: Urgent laparotomy with resection of any nonviable bowel
Water-soluble contrast study with observation for 48 hours
Nasogastric decompression and a trial of nonoperative care
Colonoscopic decompression of the proximal obstruction
items.explanation: A closed-loop obstruction with a swirl sign, mesenteric edema, and reduced enhancement indicates strangulation with a high risk of infarction. Delay increases the risk of necrosis, so prompt operation, with release of the point of obstruction and resection of nonviable bowel, is indicated. A contrast challenge and conservative care are for simple, partial adhesive obstruction without signs of ischemia.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman receives endoscopic epinephrine injection and a clip for a spurting duodenal ulcer. Eighteen hours later she vomits blood again and has a heart rate of 112, but blood pressure normalizes after 2 units of red cells. What is the best next step?
options: Immediate laparotomy with oversewing of the ulcer
Switch to an oral proton pump inhibitor and observe
Repeat endoscopy with a second attempt at hemostasis
Intravenous vasopressin infusion for splanchnic constriction
items.explanation: After initial endoscopic hemostasis, a stable patient who rebleeds should have a second endoscopic attempt, which controls bleeding in most cases and avoids operative risk. Surgery or angioembolization follows when a second attempt fails or the patient is unstable. Oral therapy is inappropriate for active bleeding, and vasopressin is used for variceal rather than ulcer hemorrhage.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman, 8 months after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, has episodes two hours after meals of sweating, tremor, and confusion. A fingerstick glucose during an episode is 46 mg/dL, and symptoms resolve when she eats. What explains these symptoms, and what is first-line management?
options: Early dumping from rapid fluid shift, treated with larger liquid meals at each sitting
Adrenal insufficiency, treated with a trial of hydrocortisone and salt loading
Marginal ulcer bleeding, treated with an endoscopic clip and transfusion
Late dumping from an insulin surge, treated with dietary carbohydrate restriction
items.explanation: Rapid delivery of carbohydrate to the jejunum triggers a large insulin surge and reactive hypoglycemia one to three hours after eating, which is late dumping. Early dumping occurs within 30 minutes with flushing, cramps, and diarrhea. First-line care is dietary, with small protein-rich meals and avoidance of simple sugars, adding acarbose if needed. Hydrocortisone and anticoagulation do not address this mechanism.

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman undergoes endoscopic mucosal resection of a nodule in Barrett esophagus. Pathology shows adenocarcinoma invading the submucosa to 900 micrometers with lymphovascular invasion and a deep margin that is involved. Which management is best?
options: Radiofrequency ablation of the remaining Barrett segment with no further resection
Esophagectomy with lymphadenectomy because of the nodal metastasis risk
Repeat endoscopy with biopsies in one year and no further treatment
High-dose proton pump inhibitor and observation with annual endoscopy
items.explanation: Submucosal invasion, especially deeper than about 500 micrometers or with lymphovascular invasion or a positive deep margin, carries a significant risk of lymph node metastasis, so endoscopic treatment is insufficient. Surgery with lymphadenectomy is recommended for fit patients. Intramucosal disease alone can be cured by resection plus ablation, but ablation alone or observation would leave unresected nodal risk.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has a mid-esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Endoscopic ultrasound shows invasion into the adventitia with two suspicious paraesophageal nodes. Computed tomography and positron emission tomography show no distant disease, and he is fit. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Primary esophagectomy followed by adjuvant observation and surveillance imaging
Endoscopic mucosal resection and annual surveillance endoscopy with biopsies
Palliative stent placement and supportive care with hospice referral
Neoadjuvant carboplatin and paclitaxel with radiation, then esophagectomy
items.explanation: A node-positive, adventitial tumor is locally advanced yet resectable. Neoadjuvant chemoradiation with carboplatin and paclitaxel, followed by surgery, improves survival and complete resection rates in both histologies and is a standard approach. Upfront surgery alone gives inferior outcomes. Endoscopic resection is only for superficial disease. Stenting is palliative and is unwarranted in a fit patient with curable disease.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has recurrent episodes of crampy abdominal pain and now small bowel intussusception. He has dark mucocutaneous freckles on the lips and buccal mucosa. Enteroscopy shows multiple hamartomatous polyps. Which statement best describes this condition?
options: APC mutation with a near-certain colorectal cancer
STK11 mutation with a high lifetime risk of cancers in several organs
MUTYH mutation with duodenal adenomas only
SMAD4 mutation with isolated juvenile polyps and no extraintestinal risk
items.explanation: Mucocutaneous freckling with hamartomatous polyps and recurrent intussusception defines Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, caused by STK11 mutation, with an elevated lifetime risk of gastrointestinal, pancreatic, breast, and gynecologic cancers. Polyps are removed by enteroscopy when large to prevent intussusception, with surveillance of multiple organs. APC, MUTYH, and SMAD4 syndromes have different polyp types and distributions. Genetic counseling is offered to relatives.

items.stem: High-resolution manometry in a 47-year-old man with dysphagia and chest pain shows incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter and spastic, premature contractions in at least a fifth of swallows, with no normal peristalsis. Barium swallow shows a corkscrew pattern above a tapered distal esophagus. Which treatment is best suited to this pattern?
options: Pneumatic balloon dilation as the single definitive treatment
Laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication without myotomy
Peroral endoscopic myotomy with an extended proximal myotomy
Botulinum toxin injection repeated every year as the long-term plan
items.explanation: This is type III achalasia, the spastic form, where the spastic segment extends above the sphincter. Myotomy that extends proximally across the spastic segment, best done by peroral endoscopic myotomy, gives the best results. Pneumatic dilation performs worst in this subtype. A complete fundoplication without myotomy would worsen obstruction. Botulinum toxin is short-lived and reserved for patients unfit for definitive therapy.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man with Crohn disease and a previous ileocecal resection has obstructive symptoms. Imaging shows three short fibrotic strictures in the jejunum, each under 10 cm, with no abscess. He has 220 cm of remaining small bowel. Which operative approach best preserves bowel length?
options: Stricturoplasty of each short stricture
Resection of the whole involved jejunum with a primary anastomosis
Bypass of the entire jejunum with an enteroenterostomy
Total proctocolectomy with end ileostomy
items.explanation: In Crohn disease with multiple short fibrotic strictures and prior resection, stricturoplasty relieves obstruction while preserving absorptive length and avoiding short bowel syndrome. Resection of long segments sacrifices bowel that will be needed over many years of disease. Bypass leaves diseased bowel with risks of bacterial overgrowth. Proctocolectomy would not treat jejunal strictures. Stricturoplasty is avoided with a phlegmon, abscess, or suspected malignancy.

items.stem: During resection of an ileal neuroendocrine tumor with hepatic metastases in a 60-year-old man, blood pressure falls to 68/40 mm Hg and bronchospasm develops after manipulation of the mass. Which intervention is most appropriate?
options: Epinephrine infusion to raise blood pressure
Large bolus of crystalloid with no other treatment
Intravenous octreotide bolus and infusion
Intravenous hydrocortisone as the only agent
items.explanation: Tumor manipulation can release large amounts of serotonin and other mediators, causing carcinoid crisis with hypotension, flushing, and bronchospasm. Intravenous somatostatin analogue is the treatment and is also given prophylactically before surgery in patients with syndrome. Catecholamines such as epinephrine can provoke further release and worsen the crisis. Fluids and steroids alone do not block mediator release.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has a gastric adenocarcinoma of the body invading the subserosa, with two enlarged perigastric nodes on computed tomography. Positron emission tomography shows no distant disease, and he is fit. Which treatment plan offers the best chance of cure?
options: Gastrectomy alone with limited nodal dissection and routine follow-up
Perioperative chemotherapy with gastrectomy and D2 lymphadenectomy
Palliative chemotherapy alone without any operation or radiation
Endoscopic submucosal dissection followed by routine surveillance
items.explanation: Resectable stage II or III gastric adenocarcinoma is treated with perioperative chemotherapy, commonly including docetaxel, oxaliplatin, and fluorouracil, along with margin-negative gastrectomy and a D2 nodal dissection performed by an experienced team. Surgery alone has poorer survival. Palliation is for metastatic disease. Endoscopic resection is limited to very early, low-risk cancers confined to the mucosa.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man with recurrent ulcers and diarrhea has an elevated fasting gastrin and a positive secretin stimulation test. Calcium is 11.4 mg/dL with an elevated parathyroid hormone, and his father had pituitary surgery. A pancreatic and duodenal mass is suspected. What is the best sequence of surgery?
options: Parathyroidectomy first, since calcium drives gastrin
Pancreaticoduodenectomy first for the suspected gastrinoma
Total gastrectomy first to remove the source of acid secretion
Pituitary resection first to lower circulating hormone levels
items.explanation: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome with hyperparathyroidism and a family history suggests multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1. Hypercalcemia stimulates gastrin release, so parathyroidectomy is performed first and often eases the ulcer disease. Gastrinomas in this syndrome are frequently multiple, small duodenal lesions, so aggressive early resection is not the first step. Total gastrectomy is now rare given proton pump inhibitor control.

items.stem: A surgeon compares acid-reducing operations for a patient with refractory duodenal ulcer who cannot take medication reliably. Which operation has the lowest rate of postoperative diarrhea and dumping, accepting a higher ulcer recurrence rate?
options: Truncal vagotomy with antrectomy
Truncal vagotomy with pyloroplasty
Subtotal gastrectomy with Billroth II reconstruction
Highly selective vagotomy
items.explanation: Highly selective, or parietal cell, vagotomy denervates only the acid-secreting fundus and preserves antral and pyloric function, so dumping and diarrhea are rare, but recurrence is higher than with other operations. Truncal vagotomy with drainage causes more diarrhea and dumping, and antrectomy adds the lowest recurrence at the cost of more side effects. A Billroth II adds bile reflux and afferent loop problems.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman will undergo retrograde cholangiopancreatography for suspected choledocholithiasis. She is young and female and has had a prior episode of pancreatitis, which places her at increased risk of post-procedure pancreatitis. Which measure best reduces that risk?
options: Prophylactic octreotide infusion for all patients
Rectal indomethacin together with generous lactated Ringer solution
Routine aggressive pancreatic duct injection of contrast
A short course of steroids before the procedure
items.explanation: Rectal nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug given around the procedure, combined with aggressive hydration using lactated Ringer solution, lowers the incidence of post-ERCP pancreatitis, and a pancreatic duct stent is added in selected high-risk cases. Octreotide and steroids have not shown reliable benefit. Repeated pancreatic duct injection raises the risk of injury and pancreatitis. Difficult cannulation is another recognized risk factor.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with cirrhosis had esophageal variceal bleeding controlled by band ligation. He is now stable on day 5 and is ready for discharge. Which plan best reduces his risk of rebleeding?
options: Proton pump inhibitor therapy alone for ulcer prevention after banding
Observation with repeat endoscopy only if bleeding recurs
A nonselective beta blocker plus repeated band ligation
Long-term octreotide infusion continued at home after discharge
items.explanation: Secondary prophylaxis after variceal bleeding combines a nonselective beta blocker, such as propranolol or nadolol, with repeated band ligation every few weeks until obliteration. Either alone is less effective than the combination. Proton pump inhibitors do not reduce variceal pressure. Waiting for another bleed has a high mortality, and octreotide is used only in the acute setting for a short time.

items.stem: Twenty-four hours after colonoscopic removal of a 3 cm flat right colon polyp using electrocautery, a 58-year-old woman has fever, localized right lower quadrant pain, and a white count of 14,000 per microliter. Her abdomen is tender but not rigid. Computed tomography shows focal wall thickening without free air. What is the diagnosis and management?
options: Free colonic perforation, managed with immediate laparotomy and repair
Delayed polypectomy bleeding, managed with angioembolization of the right colic artery
Acute appendicitis, managed with emergency appendectomy tonight
Post-polypectomy coagulation syndrome, managed with bowel rest and antibiotics
items.explanation: Transmural thermal injury without perforation produces post-polypectomy coagulation syndrome, with localized pain, fever, and leukocytosis but no free air. Most resolve with bowel rest, fluids, and antibiotics. Perforation shows free air or fluid and peritonitis and needs repair. Delayed bleeding presents with hematochezia, not pain and fever. Appendicitis would have a different imaging pattern. Close observation is needed, since free air or worsening signs would change the plan.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man has a gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. Endoscopy shows the tumor center 3 cm below the anatomic junction, involving the cardia and extending into the proximal stomach. Staging shows no distant disease. How should this tumor be classified and approached?
options: As Siewert type III, managed like gastric cancer with total gastrectomy
As a Siewert type I tumor, treated with transthoracic esophagectomy
As a Siewert type II tumor, treated only with endoscopic resection
As an esophageal squamous cancer, treated with definitive radiation alone
items.explanation: Siewert classification depends on the epicenter. Type I lies 1 to 5 cm above the junction, type II from 1 cm above to 2 cm below, and type III from 2 to 5 cm below. A subcardial tumor is type III and is managed like proximal gastric cancer, with total or extended gastrectomy and perigastric nodal dissection. Endoscopic resection is for superficial disease only, and this is an adenocarcinoma.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman with factor V Leiden has 4 days of progressive abdominal pain out of proportion to the examination. She has no peritonitis. Computed tomography shows thrombus in the superior mesenteric vein with mesenteric thickening and no free air. What is the best management?
options: Immediate laparotomy for resection of the whole involved bowel
Immediate anticoagulation, with laparotomy only for peritonitis
Aspirin alone with outpatient follow-up and discharge today
Percutaneous angioplasty of the superior mesenteric artery
items.explanation: Mesenteric venous thrombosis, often from thrombophilia, is treated with prompt anticoagulation to halt propagation and protect bowel viability. Operation is reserved for peritonitis, perforation, or infarction, with limited resection and a planned second look. Aspirin cannot treat established venous clot. Arterial angioplasty addresses the wrong vessel. Early surgery without those signs removes bowel that may recover.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man reports months of regurgitation of undigested food hours after meals, a gurgling sound in the neck, and persistent bad breath. A barium swallow shows a posterior pouch at the level of the cricoid cartilage. Through which anatomic gap does this pouch herniate?
options: The triangle between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles
The posterior wall of the distal esophagus above the diaphragm
The mid esophagus adjacent to subcarinal lymph nodes
The esophageal hiatus lateral to the right crus
items.explanation: A Zenker diverticulum is a pulsion false diverticulum that forms through the Killian triangle, a weak area between the oblique thyropharyngeus fibers and the transverse cricopharyngeus, owing to poor relaxation of the upper sphincter. Epiphrenic diverticula arise in the distal esophagus with motility disorders. Mid esophageal traction diverticula follow granulomatous nodal disease. Hiatal herniation involves the diaphragmatic opening, not the pharynx.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has an end jejunostomy with 60 cm of remaining jejunum after resection for mesenteric infarction. Despite diet changes and antimotility agents, she depends on parenteral nutrition. Which adjunct may reduce her parenteral requirement?
options: A somatostatin analogue given for every patient
Cholestyramine to bind unabsorbed bile acids in all patients
Oral long-chain fat supplements in unlimited quantity
A glucagon-like peptide-2 analogue such as teduglutide
items.explanation: In short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure, teduglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-2 analogue, promotes mucosal growth and absorption and can reduce parenteral support. Somatostatin analogues slow transit but reduce adaptation and are not first line. Cholestyramine suits an intact colon with bile acid diarrhea. An end jejunostomy needs sodium and water replacement, and unlimited fat supplements worsen steatorrhea.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a low-output enterocutaneous fistula that has not closed after eight weeks of adequate nutrition, drainage, and sepsis control. A fistulogram shows a short tract from the ileum and a stricture of the bowel distal to the opening. Which finding is the principal reason spontaneous closure is unlikely?
options: The tract is long and surrounded by an abscess cavity
The patient remains malnourished and hypoalbuminemic
Distal obstruction keeps the effluent flowing through the tract
The tract is lined by serosa rather than skin
items.explanation: Spontaneous closure of an enterocutaneous fistula is unlikely when a distal obstruction is present, along with foreign body, radiation, inflammatory bowel disease, epithelialization of the tract, abscess, or tumor. A low output, adequate nutrition, and sepsis control favor healing. Because the distal stricture diverts flow outward, surgery after nutritional optimization is usually required, typically after several months.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman has dyspepsia, and endoscopic biopsy of a gastric lesion shows an extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated tissue. She tests positive for Helicobacter pylori. Staging shows localized disease without nodal involvement. What is the initial treatment?
options: Subtotal gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy
Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy
Combination chemotherapy with rituximab
Radiation to the whole stomach
items.explanation: Low-grade gastric MALT lymphoma is driven by chronic Helicobacter pylori infection, and eradication alone produces remission in most localized cases. Patients are followed with endoscopy and biopsy. Gastrectomy is no longer a primary treatment, and chemotherapy or radiation is reserved for persistent disease after eradication, translocation-positive lymphomas, or transformation to diffuse large B cell lymphoma.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman with prior hysterectomy has crampy pain and vomiting. She has no fever or peritonitis, and computed tomography shows dilated small bowel with a transition point and no signs of ischemia. After decompression, water-soluble contrast is given. What does contrast reaching the colon by 24 hours indicate?
options: The obstruction is complete and needs urgent laparotomy
The bowel is ischemic and viability is in doubt
The obstruction will probably resolve without an operation
A closed loop is present and endoscopic stenting is needed
items.explanation: In adhesive small bowel obstruction, water-soluble contrast is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Passage into the colon within about 24 hours predicts resolution with nonoperative care and shortens hospitalization, whereas failure to reach the colon suggests the need for an operation. It does not indicate complete obstruction, ischemia, or a closed loop, which are diagnosed by clinical and imaging signs.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man completed 14 days of bismuth quadruple therapy for a Helicobacter pylori-positive duodenal ulcer four weeks ago and takes a daily proton pump inhibitor. His symptoms resolved. Which approach best confirms eradication?
options: Urea breath test after holding the proton pump inhibitor for two weeks
Urea breath test performed while he continues the proton pump inhibitor
Serum antibody titer repeated at this visit
Repeat endoscopy with no biopsy of the antrum
items.explanation: Eradication should be confirmed at least four weeks after antibiotics with a urea breath test or stool antigen, after stopping proton pump inhibitors for about two weeks because they cause false negatives. Antibody levels stay positive for months or years after cure and cannot show eradication. Endoscopy without antral biopsy provides no microbiologic information. Treatment failure is common with resistant strains, so confirmation matters.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man has a 1.5 cm well-differentiated, nonulcerated adenocarcinoma confined to the mucosa of the gastric antrum. Endoscopic ultrasound shows no submucosal invasion and no abnormal nodes. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Total gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy
Perioperative chemotherapy before distal gastrectomy
Palliative radiation to the antrum
Endoscopic submucosal dissection with en bloc resection
items.explanation: Early gastric cancers limited to the mucosa, well differentiated, small, and without ulceration or lymphovascular invasion have a very low risk of nodal metastasis and can be cured by endoscopic submucosal dissection, which allows en bloc resection with accurate pathology. Gastrectomy would be an unnecessary operation. Perioperative chemotherapy is for locally advanced disease, and radiation is not a curative method.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a 4 cm submucosal gastric mass in the body found during an evaluation for anemia. Biopsy shows spindle cells positive for KIT and DOG1, with a low mitotic rate. There is no evidence of metastasis. Which operation is appropriate?
options: Wedge resection with negative margins and no routine lymphadenectomy
Total gastrectomy with D2 lymph node dissection and omentectomy
Subtotal gastrectomy with omentectomy and splenic hilar dissection
Simple enucleation, accepting piecemeal removal through the pseudocapsule
items.explanation: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors spread hematogenously and seldom involve lymph nodes, so complete resection with negative margins, typically by wedge resection, is the aim, without routine nodal dissection. Total gastrectomy and splenectomy add morbidity without benefit. Enucleation or tumor rupture risks peritoneal seeding and recurrence. Adjuvant imatinib is considered according to size, mitotic rate, and site.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has neck pain and swelling a day after dilation of a proximal esophageal stricture. She has subcutaneous crepitus, a temperature of 38.2 C, and a heart rate of 108. Water-soluble contrast shows a small contained leak in the cervical esophagus. What is the best management?
options: Immediate right thoracotomy with primary repair of the perforation and muscle flap buttressing
Resume oral feeding with a proton pump inhibitor and outpatient review in one week
Esophagectomy with immediate gastric pull-up and a cervical anastomosis
Nothing by mouth, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and neck drainage if a collection exists
items.explanation: Small contained cervical perforations behave differently from thoracic ones because the loose neck planes drain easily and contamination of the mediastinum is limited. Most heal with fasting, antibiotics, nutrition support, and drainage of any collection. Thoracotomy and esophagectomy are excessive without a large, contaminated, or mediastinal injury. Oral intake would soil the tract and delay healing.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman with a pyloric-region gastric ulcer perforates, and laparotomy shows free spillage, a 1 cm prepyloric perforation, and mild contamination. She is hemodynamically stable. Which operative plan is most appropriate?
options: Omental patch closure alone without tissue sampling
Highly selective vagotomy with the patch repair
Omental patch closure with biopsy of the ulcer edge
Truncal vagotomy and pyloroplasty through the perforation
items.explanation: A perforated gastric ulcer carries a real chance of malignancy, so the edge must be biopsied, or the ulcer excised, when the repair is done. A patch alone risks missing cancer. Acid-reducing operations are not routinely added because Helicobacter pylori eradication and proton pump inhibition control the disease and the patient is in an emergency setting. Large or malignant lesions need resection.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman had a distal gastrectomy with Billroth II reconstruction five years ago. She now has constant epigastric pain and bilious vomiting that food does not relieve. Endoscopy shows bile in the stomach and erythematous gastritis, and the stoma is patent. What is the best surgical treatment if medical therapy fails?
options: Revision of the gastrojejunostomy to a shorter afferent loop
Conversion to Roux-en-Y reconstruction with a long Roux limb
Truncal vagotomy with a new pyloroplasty
Conversion to a loop gastrojejunostomy with a Braun enteroenterostomy only
items.explanation: Bile reflux gastritis causes pain unrelieved by meals and bilious vomiting after distal gastrectomy. Medical therapy is often ineffective, and the reliable operation is conversion to Roux-en-Y, with a limb long enough to prevent reflux. Shortening the afferent loop does not divert bile. Vagotomy does not treat reflux. A Braun anastomosis helps only partially and lacks the durable results of Roux-en-Y diversion.

items.stem: A 14-month-old boy is brought in 90 minutes after he was seen swallowing a flat, round button battery. He is drooling, and radiography shows a double-ring density at the level of the clavicles. He is breathing comfortably. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Observation at home with a stool check in two days and return precautions
Oral laxatives and a repeat radiograph after 24 hours of observation
Emergent endoscopic removal, because mucosal burns develop within hours
Magnet retrieval through a Foley catheter after a barium swallow
items.explanation: A button battery lodged in the esophagus generates current that causes liquefactive necrosis of the wall within two hours, risking perforation, fistula to the airway or aorta, and stricture. It must be removed endoscopically as an emergency, regardless of fasting status. Observation or laxatives allow ongoing injury, and barium obscures the field and delays removal. Magnet retrieval is not appropriate for a flat battery in the esophagus.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man has a squamous carcinoma at 17 cm from the incisors, in the cervical esophagus, extending to the postcricoid region. He is fit and wants to preserve his voice and swallowing. Staging shows no distant disease. What is the preferred treatment?
options: Total pharyngolaryngectomy with gastric pull-up as the first step
Transhiatal esophagectomy without any chemotherapy or radiation
Endoscopic mucosal resection followed by routine surveillance
Definitive chemoradiation with salvage surgery reserved for failure
items.explanation: Cervical esophageal squamous cancers lie close to the larynx and hypopharynx, and resection often requires laryngectomy with major functional loss. Definitive chemoradiation gives survival comparable to surgery and preserves the larynx, so it is the preferred first treatment, with salvage surgery for failure. Endoscopic resection suits only superficial disease. A transhiatal esophagectomy would not clear the proximal tumor.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man swallowed a liquid sodium hydroxide drain product with self-harm intent 6 hours ago. He is drooling but has a normal voice, a soft abdomen, and stable vital signs. Chest and abdominal radiographs show no free air. What is the best next step?
options: Upper endoscopy within the first day to grade the mucosal injury
Induced vomiting followed by an oral neutralizing solution
Barium swallow now and endoscopy after ten days
Discharge on a liquid diet with outpatient follow-up
items.explanation: In a stable patient with a caustic ingestion and no signs of perforation, endoscopy within roughly 12 to 48 hours safely grades the injury and guides feeding and surgery. Vomiting and neutralizing agents re-expose the mucosa and can generate heat. Delaying endoscopy until the stricture phase misses the chance to triage, and discharge ignores the risk of necrosis, perforation, and later stricture.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with unresectable squamous esophageal cancer reports cough every time he swallows liquids, and recurrent pneumonia. Bronchoscopy confirms a fistula between the midesophagus and the left main bronchus. What is the best palliative intervention?
options: An uncovered self-expanding metal stent across the tumor
A covered self-expanding metal stent across the fistula
Dilation of the tumor and resumption of oral intake
Feeding gastrostomy alone with continued oral liquids
items.explanation: A malignant tracheoesophageal or bronchoesophageal fistula is best sealed with a covered self-expanding stent, which restores swallowing and stops aspiration. An uncovered stent lets tumor and fluid pass through the fistula and does not seal it. Dilation alone leaves the opening, and oral intake would worsen aspiration. A gastrostomy gives access for feeding but must be paired with stopping oral intake.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman has sudden severe epigastric and lower chest pain with repeated unproductive retching. A nasogastric tube will not pass. Chest radiography shows a retrocardiac air-fluid level. She is afebrile with a heart rate of 104 and blood pressure of 128/76 mm Hg. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Urgent operative reduction of the stomach with hernia repair and gastropexy
Observation with serial abdominal examinations and a clear liquid diet
Endoscopic dilation of the hiatus followed by bowel rest and antiemetics
Elective fundoplication after outpatient barium study and manometry
items.explanation: Pain, unproductive retching, and inability to pass a tube form the Borchardt triad of acute gastric volvulus within a paraesophageal hernia. Ischemia and perforation can follow quickly, so urgent decompression, reduction, sac excision, crural repair, and gastropexy are indicated. Observation risks necrosis. Endoscopic dilation does not address the anatomy. Elective studies and fundoplication are appropriate only for stable, chronic symptoms.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman has mild gallstone pancreatitis that is improving. Liver enzymes are mildly elevated, and transabdominal ultrasound cannot see the distal bile duct, so she has an intermediate probability of a common duct stone. She wants to avoid an unnecessary therapeutic procedure. Which test is most appropriate?
options: Immediate retrograde cholangiopancreatography with sphincterotomy
Repeat transabdominal ultrasound in one month
Endoscopic ultrasound or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography
Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography
items.explanation: For intermediate-probability choledocholithiasis, a less invasive diagnostic study such as endoscopic ultrasound or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography identifies stones accurately and avoids the risks of an unnecessary retrograde procedure. Immediate retrograde cholangiopancreatography is for high probability or cholangitis. Waiting leaves the question unanswered, and transhepatic cholangiography is invasive and reserved for failure of other routes. Positive findings can then be treated in a single therapeutic session.

items.stem: On the third day after esophagectomy with a neck anastomosis, a 66-year-old man has a hoarse, breathy voice and coughs when he drinks. Laryngoscopy shows an immobile left vocal cord in the paramedian position. Which event most likely explains this finding?
options: Anastomotic leak with a mediastinal abscess compressing the larynx
Left recurrent laryngeal nerve injury during mediastinal dissection
Thoracic duct injury with chylothorax from the mediastinal dissection
Gastric conduit ischemia at the tip of the conduit near the anastomosis
items.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops beneath the aortic arch and ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove, making it vulnerable during cervical and upper mediastinal dissection and nodal clearance. Vocal cord paralysis causes hoarseness and aspiration. A leak or conduit ischemia produces sepsis or systemic signs rather than isolated cord immobility, and a chyle leak causes high-volume drainage.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman has recurrent melena and iron deficiency anemia. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy, including terminal ileum intubation, are normal. She has had no abdominal surgery or obstructive symptoms. What is the most appropriate next test?
options: Repeat colonoscopy within one week
Exploratory laparotomy with intraoperative enteroscopy
Barium enteroclysis as the first test
Video capsule endoscopy of the small bowel
items.explanation: After a negative upper and lower endoscopy, suspected small bowel bleeding is evaluated first with video capsule endoscopy, which is noninvasive and has a high diagnostic yield when performed early. A stricture risk should be excluded first, as a capsule can be retained. Repeating the same endoscopies adds little, laparotomy is reserved for failure of less invasive methods, and barium studies are less sensitive for vascular lesions.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has regurgitation and a chronic cough that persist despite twice-daily acid suppression. Upper endoscopy is normal and she asks about an antireflux operation. Which evaluation is needed before considering surgery?
options: Manometry plus ambulatory pH monitoring performed off acid suppression
Repeat endoscopy with random biopsies every year for the next five years
Barium swallow alone to look for a hiatal hernia and measure its size
A further trial of higher-dose acid suppression with no objective testing before surgery
items.explanation: With a normal endoscopy and poor response to acid suppression, reflux must be proved objectively before surgery. Ambulatory pH testing off therapy confirms pathologic acid exposure, and manometry excludes achalasia or severe motility failure that would make a fundoplication harmful and guides the choice of wrap. Barium swallow cannot quantify reflux. Repeating endoscopy or escalating the dose does not provide proof.

items.stem: On the third day after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, a 38-year-old woman has fever, heart rate of 124, and left upper quadrant pain radiating to the shoulder. Computed tomography with oral contrast shows extraluminal contrast near the angle of His. Where is the most common site of this complication?
options: The distal staple line at the antrum
The proximal staple line near the gastroesophageal junction
The jejunojejunostomy
The gastrojejunal anastomosis
items.explanation: Leaks after sleeve gastrectomy occur most often at the proximal staple line near the angle of His, where tissue is thick, the pressure is highest, and blood supply is limited. A stable patient may be managed with drainage, stenting, and nutrition, whereas instability needs reoperation. A jejunojejunostomy and a gastrojejunostomy exist only after bypass, not in a sleeve.

items.stem: A 43-year-old man has a body mass index of 32 kg per square meter and type 2 diabetes that is poorly controlled despite two agents and insulin. He is motivated and has no contraindication. Under current consensus guidance, how should his candidacy for metabolic surgery be viewed?
options: He is excluded, since the threshold is a BMI of 35 or more in all patients
He is excluded until he first loses 10 percent of body weight by diet alone
He qualifies only for an adjustable gastric band, not other operations
He may be considered, since BMI of 30 to 34.9 with diabetes qualifies
items.explanation: Current guidance from major bariatric and metabolic societies recommends surgery for BMI of 35 or more regardless of comorbidity, and recommends considering it for BMI of 30 to 34.9 with metabolic disease such as diabetes. Mandatory prior weight loss is not required. The band is rarely chosen now, and the procedure is selected through shared decision making rather than a fixed rule.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman who smokes has epigastric pain eight months after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Endoscopy shows a 1 cm ulcer at the gastrojejunal anastomosis on the jejunal side. Besides acid suppression with sucralfate, what is the most important modifiable intervention?
options: Starting a daily bisphosphonate for bone protection
Increasing the portion size to buffer the acid
Stopping tobacco and avoiding nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Converting immediately to a sleeve gastrectomy
items.explanation: Marginal ulcers form at the gastrojejunostomy, and the main modifiable risks are smoking and anti-inflammatory drug use, with ischemia and tension also contributing. Cessation together with proton pump inhibitor and sucralfate therapy heals most. Larger meals do not buffer a jejunal ulcer. Bisphosphonates can injure the mucosa. A sleeve conversion is not a treatment for an ulcer and is rarely performed.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with Barrett esophagus undergoes surveillance endoscopy with four-quadrant biopsies. Two independent expert pathologists agree on low-grade dysplasia in a flat segment, and no visible nodule is present. He is fit for any intervention. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
options: Esophagectomy with gastric pull-up within the next month
Endoscopic eradication with radiofrequency ablation of the Barrett segment
Repeat endoscopy in five years without any treatment
Antireflux fundoplication alone with no further endoscopic therapy
items.explanation: Confirmed low-grade dysplasia carries a meaningful annual progression risk, so guidelines favor endoscopic eradication, most often radiofrequency ablation, over surveillance alone. Esophagectomy is excessive for flat low-grade disease. A five-year interval fits nondysplastic Barrett only. Fundoplication controls reflux but does not remove dysplastic epithelium or reliably prevent progression, so ablation is still needed. Surveillance intervals are shortened, never lengthened, once dysplasia is confirmed.

items.stem: During appendectomy in a 35-year-old man, a Meckel diverticulum is found incidentally 60 cm from the ileocecal valve. Which finding at palpation most strongly favors resection?
options: Palpable thickening suggesting ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue
A thin, soft diverticulum with a wide base and no palpable thickening
A short diverticulum less than 1 cm with a broad base
A normal-appearing diverticulum in a patient older than 60 years
items.explanation: Features that favor resection of an incidental Meckel diverticulum include palpable thickening or a mass suggesting heterotopic gastric or pancreatic mucosa, a narrow neck, longer length, or an associated band, because these predict later bleeding or obstruction. A soft, wide-based, short diverticulum carries little risk. Older age lowers the lifetime benefit of resection, so a normal diverticulum is more often left alone.

items.stem: A surgeon mobilizes the cervical esophagus during a neck exploration and wants to preserve its blood supply. Which artery is the dominant source of supply to this segment?
options: Left gastric artery
Bronchial arteries arising from the descending aorta
Inferior thyroid artery
Inferior phrenic artery
items.explanation: The cervical esophagus is supplied mainly by branches of the inferior thyroid artery. The thoracic esophagus receives segmental supply from bronchial arteries and direct aortic branches, and the abdominal portion is supplied by the left gastric and inferior phrenic arteries. The segmental, watershed nature of this supply explains why a gastric conduit based on the right gastroepiploic artery is vulnerable at its tip.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with no cardiac disease is admitted with upper gastrointestinal bleeding from a duodenal ulcer, and endoscopy is scheduled within 24 hours. He is hemodynamically stable with a hemoglobin of 6.8 g/dL. What is the best transfusion strategy?
options: Liberal strategy, transfusing for a hemoglobin below 10 g/dL
Transfuse only if hemoglobin falls below 5 g/dL or he becomes symptomatic
Transfuse two units of platelets and plasma before endoscopy
Restrictive strategy, transfusing below 7 g/dL to maintain 7 to 9 g/dL
items.explanation: In acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding without cardiovascular disease, a restrictive transfusion threshold of 7 g/dL, targeting 7 to 9, lowers rebleeding and mortality compared with a liberal approach, since overtransfusion raises portal and arterial pressure. Waiting for 5 g/dL is unsafe, and platelet transfusion has no role with a normal platelet count. Patients with cardiac disease or instability need individualized higher thresholds.
